statement: As described in one scoping review (Kheirkhah et al., 2024; searched to December 2023; the included studies were not appraised, so its figures are second-hand), evidence is insufficient to say whether music changes how a ketamine or esketamine session goes. The review found 14 studies of music with ketamine, all in patients in clinical or trial settings. In nine, ketamine was given with other sedatives or painkillers, during procedures or, in one study, air medical transport; in most of them music went with less sedation or drug use and lower anxiety, pain or fear, but one trial found no effect on emergence reactions and another found more dreams or emergence reactions with music, though no unpleasant dreams, against 10 controls with unpleasant dreams. Of the five studies of ketamine or esketamine alone, only one compared people who listened with people who heard nothing: in 46 children having heart catheterization under ketamine anaesthesia, the 23 who heard recordings of their mothers' voices (musical in 12 of them) had less anxiety before the procedure and fewer emergence reactions than 23 who wore headphones with no recording. The other four were case reports and interview studies without such a comparison: a woman on esketamine nasal spray found that music of her choice helped with dissociation, confusion and anxiety; two patients with bipolar depression tolerated dissociation better with preferred music in later infusions, which may reflect getting used to the infusions; in 12 people given ketamine in a trial for alcohol use disorder, everyone who listened to music heard it distorted in speed and pitch, felt as good or bad depending on their state; and in 17 people on oral esketamine for depression, music was described as blocking distractions and helping inner exploration, but some felt it kept them tied to the outside world and one stopped using it. Up to its search, the review found no study comparing music with no music during ketamine or esketamine treatment for depression, and its own limitations say no conclusions can be drawn; a randomized clinical trial of music with ketamine for depression published after that search (Greenway et al., 2024) has not yet been read for this answer. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: A review found 14 studies of music with ketamine, all with patients. Most gave ketamine together with other medicines, usually during surgery or tests; in most of these, music went with less worry or pain. Only one study of ketamine alone compared listening with silence: children who heard their mother's voice were less anxious. The review, searched to the end of 2023, found no study comparing music with no music during ketamine treatment for depression, so it is not known whether music helps; a trial published in 2024 has not been read here yet.
population: Patients given ketamine or esketamine in clinical settings (anaesthesia, sedation, depression and alcohol-use-disorder treatment), in 14 studies gathered by a scoping review
exposure: Music (or, in one trial, recordings of mothers' voices) before, during or after ketamine or esketamine
comparator: No music (headphones with no recording, or a blank soundtrack) in most procedural trials and in the one comparison of ketamine alone; no comparison in the case reports and interview studies
outcome: Anxiety, pain, emergence reactions, sedative use, dissociation and how the session was experienced
magnitude: No pooled estimates. 14 studies: 9 with other sedatives (music with less sedation and lower anxiety or pain in most; no effect on emergence reactions in one; more dreams or emergence reactions in another); 5 with ketamine or esketamine alone, one comparing listeners with children who heard nothing (46 children: mothers' voices against headphones with no recording), the rest case reports (3 patients) and interview studies (17 and 12 people). No study comparing music with no music during ketamine treatment for depression up to December 2023.

risk_of_bias.note: The included studies were not appraised by the review and cannot be appraised here; whether music was randomly allocated is stated for one study; the review's highlights state benefits that its limitations disclaim (card sc_kheirkhah_2024).

inconsistency.note: Directions vary between procedural trials (one null, one with more dreams or emergence reactions), as the statement says.

indirectness.note: Second-hand (METHODS §6.3); most studies gave ketamine with other sedatives during procedures, often in children, and the only controlled ketamine-alone study used mothers' voices, partly spoken.

grade.reasoning: For the question asked (music in ketamine sessions), the primary evidence the review describes is small trials of unstated design, case reports and interview studies, so it starts low; down one for risk of bias (not appraisable) and one for indirectness (second-hand, procedural, with other drugs), giving very low. Status single study: for ketamine or esketamine alone the review found one comparison of listening with no listening (46 children under anaesthesia, hearing recordings of their mothers' voices), seen through one review; the procedural trials gave ketamine with other drugs. The claim rests only on a scoping review, recorded as a narrative review, so it stays at draft (METHODS §6.3). A randomized clinical trial of music with ketamine for depression (Greenway et al., 2024, on the project's list) appeared after the review's search; it has no card in this round, and this answer should be revisited when it has been read.
